title.en: The Bride with Forty Champions: Nila Panchadi Comes to Singhapura
title.zh: 四十勇士護嫁的妮拉潘佳蒂

region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. IV (marriage of Raja Kichil Besar), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja of Bijanagar in the land of Kling refuses all suitors for his peerless daughter Nila Panchadi, 'as not being of her own race' — until word of the Singhapura dynasty, descended from Raja Suran, reaches him. He sends her north with forty champions in a vessel of five hundred rowers; three months of festivities precede the wedding, and Singhapura's line is joined to the kings of the land of Kling.
summary.zh: 克林國比賈那伽王拒絕一切求婚者——『非同族者不嫁』絕世之女妮拉潘佳蒂；獨聞獅城王系亦出蘇蘭王之裔，乃遣五百槳巨舟、四十勇士護女北上。歡宴三月，公主下嫁獅城王子——兩王世系自此相連。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle alliance episode; the 'same race' clause mirrors Sang Sapurba's endogamy myth (batch-217).

passages.text: There was a raja of the land of Kling, Adi Bernilam Raja Mudeliar, descended of Raja Suran, who had a daughter named Nila Panchadi, of celebrated beauty and most excellent qualities. How many were the rajas who preferred their suit to her, but her father refused to give her in marriage to them, as not being of her own race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. IV (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the fame of her beauty reached Singhapura, and Sri Tri-buana sent ambassadors to solicit her hand for his son Raja Kichil Besar. The raja of Bijanagar rejoiced at the letter, desiring that the prince should not take the trouble of coming, but that he would send his daughter to Singhapura. The next monsoon she sailed attended by forty champions in a vessel equipped with five hundred rowers, and after three months of festivities the prince was united to the Kling princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. IV (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wood-Shaving Ring: Java's Letter of Contempt and the Hatchet Answer
title.zh: 刨花之環：爪哇的辱信與斧頭的回敬

region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. V (the shaving of wood), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The bitara of Majapahit sends Singhapura a letter enclosing a wood-shaving seven fathoms long, hewn fine as paper and rolled up like a ring: 'Younger brother, observe the skill of the artificers of Java; have you any such in Singhapura?' The raja answers with a greater wonder — his artificer Pawang Bentan shaves the head of a forty-day-old boy with a hatchet, unharmed, amid the rolling of the child's head. The insulted bitara reads the point: 'he threatens to shave our head like the boy's' — and sends a hundred junks to war.
summary.zh: 馬卓帕希特王致獅城一函，內附刨花一條，長七尋，薄如紙、捲之成環：『賢弟且觀爪哇工匠之技；獅城可有此等人物？』獅城王答以更奇之技——工匠帕旺·本丹以斧為四十日嬰兒剃頭，嬰啼哭轉首而毫髮無傷。馬卓王讀其意：『彼欲如剃嬰般剃我首級』——遂發百艘戰船而來。

sensitivity.note: Famous insult-and-answer challenge episode; a classic 'boast contest' (jurus) motif in Malay-Javan court legend.

passages.text: The bitara of Majapahit sent an ambassador to Singhapura with a letter enclosing a shaving of wood, seven fathoms in length, formed with the hatchet, fine as paper, and nowhere cut or broken; it was rolled up and its circumference like a ring. The letter read: 'Younger brother, observe the skill of the artificers of Java; have you any such in Singhapura?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sri Paduca Vicrama Vira ordered the artificer Pawang Bentan to hew off the hair from the head of a boy of forty days old with a hatchet in the presence of the ambassador of Java. The artificer executed his commission without delay, notwithstanding the exertions of the boy and the constant rolling motion of his head, to the great astonishment of the Javanese ambassador. 'To shave a boy's head with a hatchet is somewhat more difficult than to pare off your shaving,' said the raja; 'carry this axe to Majapahit with our compliments.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sri Bitara was highly enraged at the narrative. 'I understand the raja's meaning; he threatens to shave our head like the boy's, if we should proceed to Singhapura.' Without delay he ordered his warriors to proceed in a hundred junks to Singhapura and attack it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hundred Junks of Majapahit Break Against Singhapura
title.zh: 百艦來犯：馬卓帕希特兵敗獅城

region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. V (the Javanese attack), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: A hundred junks under the champion Damang Viraja land Javanese warriors on Singhapura: 'there was clattering of arms on armour, and the earth shook with the stamping of warriors, and loud rose the hubbub of contending hosts.' Blood streams on the ground till evening, when the Javans fall back to their prows; Singhapura is not worsted, and the hosts return to Majapahit.
summary.zh: 馬卓王遣百艘大船，載名將達萬·維拉查之爪哇兵登岸攻獅城：『甲葉相擊聲不絕，戰士踏地地為震，兩軍喧囂聲蓋天。』血染大地直至日暮，爪哇兵退回船中；獅城未敗，敵軍歸國。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle battle set-piece; Singhapura's repulse of Majapahit.

passages.text: The fleet which the bitara sent under the command of the famous champion Damang Viraja arrived at Singhapura, and the Javan warriors immediately rushed ashore and commenced the war with the people of Singhapura.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thick waxed the press of war, there was clattering of arms on armour, and the earth shook with the stamping of warriors, and loud rose the hubbub of contending hosts, so that no other noise could be heard. Many were the slain on both sides, and the blood streamed on the ground till evening, when the Javans fell back to their prows. Singhapura, however, was not worsted; the Javan hosts returned to Majapahit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

region.en: Sungey Basisi, Sayang country near Singhapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獅城附近斯揚之地之鱗河（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the champion Badang), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The slave Badang's fish-snare is emptied night after night, leaving only scales and bones. Watching among the reeds he seizes the glutton — a hantu with eyes red as fire and beard hanging to its navel — and bargains: not riches, which would belong to his master, but strength 'to rend up by the roots trees of one or two fathoms girt.' The spectre's price is terrible: Badang must lick up its vomit. He swallows it while gripping the beard, shivers the forest with a wave of his hand, and earns his freedom.
summary.zh: 奴隸巴當的魚梁夜夜被吃空，只餘鱗骨。他藏身蘆葦之中，擒住那食魚之魅——雙目如火、鬚垂至臍的鬼。鬼願獻禮求生：巴當不取財富（歸主人所有），而求『徒手連根拔起一兩尋粗之樹』之力。鬼言：須先食其嘔物。巴當緊握鬼鬚吞之，從此揮手之間森林盡倒，並以此換得自由身。

sensitivity.note: Strength-through-monster bargain; the Badang cycle is one of the Annals' folk-epic insets.

passages.text: Badang had set in the river a snare for fish; on going next morning to examine it he found no fish, but the scales and bones of them. The same occurred for several days, when he concealed himself one night among the reeds, and saw a hantu, or spectre, with eyes red as fire, hair coarse and matted as a basket, and beard hanging down to his navel, come to eat the fish that were caught. He made his heart strong and rushed to seize it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'If I should desire riches,' thought Badang, 'they would all belong to my master; but if I ask for strength to perform my master's business, that would be of some advantage. Give me strength, so that I may rend up with one hand by the roots trees of one or two fathoms girt.' The hantu consented on a condition: 'provided you can agree to lick up my vomit.' Badang vomited it up and swallowed it, holding the spectre by the beard, and then tried his hand on the largest trees, shivering them to pieces with the greatest facility.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: He returned to his master's dwelling, shivering all the trees before him and clearing away the brushwood with the waving of his hand, till he had cleared away the deep forest almost like a plain. When his master inquired what faculty he had for the purpose, Badang related the whole affair, and thereupon received his freedom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Batu Blah: The Stone Split by Badang's Falling Head
title.zh: 裂石：巴當之頭劈開巨石

region.zh: 柔佛海岸瓜拉斯揚（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the split stone), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Summoned to fetch the kuras leaf of Cowala Sayang for his raja, Badang rows a prow of eight fathoms alone, using a campas-tree trunk a fathom in girth for an oar. Climbing for the leaf, the branch breaks and he falls head-first onto a huge stone, splitting it in two — 'but not his skull.' The split stone, Batu Blah, and even his prodigious oar, are pointed out to travellers for generations after.
summary.zh: 王欲食瓜拉斯揚之古拉斯葉，巴當獨自划八尋長舟前往，以一尋粗之坎帕斯樹幹作槳。攀樹摘葉，枝折墜地——頭撞巨石，石裂為二，『而顱骨無恙』。裂石（巴都布拉）與其巨槳，世代為旅人指認之古蹟。

passages.text: The raja of Singhapura wished to eat of the kuras leaf, which grows at Cowala Sayang, and Badang departed alone in a prow eight fathoms in length, with a trunk of the campas tree for an oar, which was a fathom in girt. When he reached Cowala Sayang he ascended the kuras tree; but the branch broke with him, and he fell down with his head on a huge stone, which stone was split in two, but not his skull.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: This stone is still to be seen at Cowala Sayang, and is named Batu Blah, or the split stone; and the said prow, with the trunk of the tree which he used for an oar, are still to be seen at Cowala Sayang. Badang returned to Singhapura the next day, bringing with him a cargo of plantains and sugar-canes for his food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Badang Launches the Fifteen-Fathom Prow with One Hand
title.zh: 巴當獨力推動十五尋巨舟

region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the launching of the pilang), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja builds a great pilang prow of fifteen fathoms and orders it launched. Fifty men fail; two or three hundred fail; two or three thousand fail. Then the raja calls Badang, who launches it with such force that it flies straight across to the opposite shore — and the king appoints him a hulubalang, a champion, whose fame reaches even the land of Kling.
summary.zh: 王造十五尋巨舟命人下水：五十人不動，二三百人不動，二三千人不動。王乃召巴當——他一推之下，巨舟飛越水面直達對岸。王遂封之為呼魯巴蘭（戰將），其名遠播克林之地。

sensitivity.note: Feat-of-strength episode in the Badang cycle.

passages.text: The raja of Singhapura constructed a prow of the kind named Pilang, fifteen fathoms in length, at the raja's residence. When it was finished he ordered fifty men to launch it, but they were unable; it was then essayed by two or three hundred, and afterwards by two or three thousand, all of whom were unable to succeed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the raja ordered Badang to attempt it alone, and he launched it with such force that it flew directly to the opposite shore. After this exploit the king appointed him a champion, or hulubalang, and his fame extended even to the land of Kling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stone Hurl of Badang: Seven Ships Staked and Lost
title.zh: 巴當舉石定輸贏：七船為注

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (Badang and the Kling champion), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The Kling champion Nadi Vijaya Vicrama arrives to wrestle Badang, staking seven loaded ships on the outcome. Evenly matched at play, they turn to the huge stone before the raja's hall: the Kling champion can barely raise it to his knee, but Badang poises it easily several times and hurls it into the mouth of the river — 'that is the rock which is at this day visible at the point of Singhapura.' The challenger surrenders his seven ships in shame.
summary.zh: 克林勇士納迪·維賈亞渡海來摔跤，以七艘滿載之船為注。二人相持不下，遂約舉王殿前巨石分高下：克林勇士僅能舉至膝而放；巴當卻輕鬆拋舉數次，擲石入河口——『即今日獅城岬外所見之礁石』。挑戰者羞愧獻上七船而歸。

sensitivity.note: Wrestling-and-stone feat; the Annals ties the rock at Singapore point to Badang's throw.

passages.text: There was in the land of Kling a champion of such amazing force that nobody could venture to contend with him, named Nadi Vijaya Vicrama. Hearing of the prowess of Badang, the raja of Kling sent him to Singhapura to contend in wrestling, staking seven ships with their loading on the issue of the contest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a huge stone lying before the raja's hall, and the Kling champion said to Badang: 'Let us come to a serious exertion of strength, and lift up this stone; let him be reckoned worsted who shall be unable to lift it.' The Kling champion exerted all his strength and lifted it up to his knee and let it fall. Badang took up the stone, poised it easily several times, and threw it out into the mouth of the river — that is the rock which is at this day visible at the point of Singhapura.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Kling champion delivered up to Badang the seven ships which had been staked with their contents, and owned that he was conquered. He returned with great sorrow and shame to the land of Kling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Knee at the Feast: Badang Unmanned the Champion Bandrang
title.zh: 宴席上的膝蓋：巴當暗中壓服班德朗

region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (Bandrang of Perlac), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Bandrang, the redoubtable champion of Perlac, comes to stake a storehouse against Badang. Warned by his raja not to despair, Badang asks that the challenger be invited to a feast first: seated together, Bandrang presses his knee down on Badang's — and Badang, quick as thought, presses down his, so secretly that no one sees. A silent hour of locked knees breaks the champion: next morning the ambassador begs to cancel the contest, and Badang is instead set to fixing a great iron chain across the strait.
summary.zh: 珀拉克勇士班德朗前來，以一倉貨物為注挑戰巴當。巴當請王先設宴款客；席間二人並坐，班德朗以膝下壓——巴當閃電般回壓其膝，隱秘無人察覺。對坐一時，勇士之膝已被鎖死。翌晨使臣請求罷賽；巴當未戰而勝，改被派去橫鎖海峽之鐵鏈。

sensitivity.note: Silent contest-of-strength at table — a celebrated Malay narrative device.

passages.text: Badang represented that Bandrang was the most powerful champion of the time, and that no one was reckoned equal to him; 'if therefore I should be conquered, do not be disconcerted: it may be best for you to invite him this evening to an entertainment, when I shall endeavour to discover if I can contend with him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bandrang and Badang were seated together. Bandrang immediately pressed his knee down upon that of Badang, but Badang quickly extricated himself, and having raised his own knee pressed down that of Bandrang, who could not, with all his efforts, raise his knee: this was done so secretly that none observed it except themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the ambassador asked that the contest be put off altogether, as it might possibly excite dissatisfaction between the two rajas; Bandrang had requested him to find some method of breaking off the contest, for he perceived his strength to be inferior. The raja smiled and assented, and instead set Badang to fix a large and heavy iron chain behind the strait of Sri Kama to prevent the passing of vessels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Two Stone Pillars from Kling over Badang's Grave
title.zh: 克林王送石柱於巴當之墓

region.en: Point of the straits of Singhapura

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (Badang's death), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Badang dies he is buried at the point of the straits of Singhapura. Tidings reach the land of Kling, whose raja sends two stone pillars to be raised over the grave as a monument — 'these are the pillars which are still at the point of the bay.' Even in death, the Annals insists, the strongman's fame draws honours from across the sea.
summary.zh: 巴當死，葬於獅城海峽之岬。訊至克林，其王遣二石柱豎於墓上為紀念——『即今灣岬之石柱』。壯士雖死，其名跨海受祭。

sensitivity.note: Grave-monument etiology closing the Badang cycle.

passages.text: After a long time, Badang also died, and was buried at the point of the straits of Singhapura, and when the tidings of his death reached the land of Kling, the raja sent two stone pillars, to be raised over his grave as a monument, and these are the pillars which are still at the point of the bay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Barnacles Turned to Gold: Marah Silu of Pasangan
title.zh: 藤壺化金：帕桑甘的馬拉·西魯

region.en: Pasangan, Samudra coast, north Sumatra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘三摩陀海岸帕桑甘（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (Marah Silu's gold), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The fish-weir keeper Marah Silu keeps finding kalang-kalang (barnacles) in his traps and casting them back — until, enraged, he boils them: the barnacles turn to gold and the foam of the boiling water to silver. His brother Marah Chaka, told that Silu 'eats barnacles,' seeks to kill him; Silu flees to the forest of Jaran and wins followers by giving away gold — the obscure fisherman fated to become the first sultan of Samudra.
summary.zh: 設魚梁的馬拉·西魯屢屢在梁中拾得藤壺，丟回海中又復出現；怒而煮之——藤壺化金、煮水之沫化銀。兄長馬拉·查卡聞『弟食藤壺』欲殺之；西魯逃入查蘭森林，散金收眾——賤業漁人注定成為三摩陀首位蘇丹。

sensitivity.note: Low-born founder tested by rumour (the 'barnacle-eater' slander) before exaltation.

passages.text: Marah Silu gained his livelihood by keeping fish-weirs on the shore of the sea, and he repeatedly found in them kalang-kalang, or biche de Mar, which he rejected into the sea; no sooner had he adjusted his weirs, but he found they had returned. He got angry and boiled them, when the kalang-kalang were converted into gold, while the foam of the water in which they had been boiled was converted into silver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last Marah Chaka was informed that his brother Marah Silu was in the habit of eating kalang-kalang, and was enraged and wanted to kill him. When Marah Silu heard of this intention he fled to the forest of Jaran, where he lived a long time and gave liberally of the gold he had acquired to all the people in his vicinity, and they all became obedient to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ant as Big as a Cat: The Naming of Samatra
title.zh: 大如貓的螞蟻：三摩陀之名

region.zh: 北蘇門答臘瑟馬德拉丘

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the great ant), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Hunting from his forest refuge, Marah Silu's dog Sipasei gives tongue on an eminence; ascending, Silu finds a huge ant as large as a cat — and eats it. He makes the hill his residence and names it Semadra, 'the great ant' (semut raya): the name from which, the Annals says, comes Samatra (Sumatra), the island promised in a hadis as a land that would one day 'produce many Wali-alah.'
summary.zh: 馬拉·西魯行獵，犬西帕塞於丘上吠叫；登丘見一巨蟻，大如貓——遂食之。即以該丘為居，名之『瑟馬德拉』，意即『大螞蟻』（semut raya）——《紀年》云：蘇門答臘之名即由此而來，並引聖訓言此地將出眾多聖徒。

sensitivity.note: Name-etiology for Sumatra; entomophagy as royal omen.

passages.text: On a certain day Marah Silu went a hunting, and his dog Sipasei gave tongue on an elevated piece of ground. When Marah Silu had ascended the eminence, he observed a huge ant which was as large as a cat; he took this ant and ate it, and this eminence he made his residence, and named it Semadra, which signifies the great ant (semut raya).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is related in the hadis of the prophet Muhammed that he said to his companions: 'In the latter times men shall hear of an island under the wind, named Samadra; as soon as this shall happen, go and convert it to Islamism, for the island shall produce many Wali-alah, or persons of gifted piety.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fakir's Test: Only Samadra Could Read the Koran
title.zh: 苦行僧之試：惟三摩陀能誦古蘭

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the conversion of Marah Silu), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Fulfilling the hadis, the sharif of Mecca sends a vessel with a fakir disguised in it — Sultan Muhammed of Matabar, descended from Abubacar. Sailing from Pasuri through Lambri and Haru, he offers the Koran at every land and none can read it, until at Samadra the fisherman Marah Silu, after the prophet spat into his mouth in a dream, reads it aloud. The hidden sultan installs him as Sultan Malac al Salih — the Annals' conversion miracle of Sumatra's first Islamic sultanate.
summary.zh: 應聖訓，麥加謝里夫遣船，船中偽裝之苦行僧乃馬塔巴爾蘇丹穆罕默德（出自阿布·巴克爾之裔）。沿途經帕蘇里、蘭布里、哈魯，出示古蘭，皆無人能誦；至三摩陀，漁人馬拉·西魯——夢中先知唾其口——朗誦經文。隱姓之王遂冊立之，號『馬立克·薩利赫』——此即蘇門答臘首個伊斯蘭蘇丹國之皈依神蹟。

sensitivity.note: Conversion legend of the Annals; respectful treatment of an Islamic hagiographic episode.

passages.text: Then the sheref of Mecca sent a vessel properly fitted out, and ordered the mariners to proceed to the land of Samadra. They reached the land of Matabar, where a raja named Sultan Muhammed, descended from Abubacar, appointed his eldest son to the government and embarked in the guise of a fakir, desiring them to convey him to the land of Samadra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a long voyage they arrived at the land of Pasuri, the whole of the inhabitants of which embraced Islamism; the fakir went ashore carrying the Koran and presented it to the people to read, but not one of them could read it. The same happened at Lambri and at Haru. When Marah Silu went to sleep he dreamed that he was face to face with the holy prophet, who desired him to open his mouth, on which the prophet spat into it, and he immediately awaked, when his body had the odour of Narawastu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the morning came the fakir landed and ordered Marah Silu to read the Koran, and he read it. Then the fakir said to Sheikh Ismail, the nakhoda: 'This is the land of Samadra, mentioned by the holy prophet.' Sheikh Ismail landed all the royal accoutrements he had brought, and installed Marah Silu as raja, under the title of Sultan Malec al Salih.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: Putri Ganggang Seated Highest: The Envoy Who Chose the Concubine's Daughter
title.zh: 最高處的邦邦公主：使者選中庶女

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the embassy for a bride), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sultan Malac al Salih sends Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din to Perlac to ask a raja's daughter in marriage. The raja seats his two legitimate daughters undermost and the concubine's daughter, Putri Ganggang, above them, rosy in water-jambu colours, ordering her to open betel for her sisters. Asked which lady he seeks, the envoy unknowingly answers 'the one who sits uppermost' — and the laughing raja grants her: her black-sheep elevation becomes a marriage into the Samudra throne.
summary.zh: 馬立克·薩利赫遣使赴珀拉克求親。珀拉克王使二嫡女坐於下，庶出之女邦邦公主獨坐高處，身著玫瑰色衣，命為二妹剖檳榔。使者不知內情，言：『我求坐在最高處之小姐』——王大笑允嫁。庶女之『僭位』反成三摩陀王室聯姻。

sensitivity.note: Seating-test betrothal episode (the low-born bride raised to honor).

passages.text: The raja of Perlac had three daughters, two of whom were legitimate, and one by a concubine, named Putri Ganggang; he showed all three to Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din, seating the two legitimate daughters undermost, and the natural daughter above them in a more elevated place, and ordered her to open betelnut for her sisters. She was dressed in rosy-coloured clothes, with a vest of the colour of the water jambu, with earrings like the young palm leaf, and looked extremely handsome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then said Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din, 'I ask the young lady who sits uppermost;' but he did not know that she was the natural daughter of the raja. Then loud laughed the raja, saying, 'Whichever of them you please, you are welcome to her.' He ordered a hundred prows to be prepared and sent Putri Ganggang to the land of Samadra, where the marriage was consummated after several days of splendid entertainments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the founding of Pasei), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Perlac is conquered and refugees flee to Samudra, Sultan Malac al Salih resolves to found a settlement for his two sons. Crossing the river on his elephant Parmadewan, his dog Sipasei gives tongue; he finds a piece of elevated ground 'as if it had been levelled,' clears it, builds a town — and names it Pasei after the dog. His eldest son is made its raja and the royal possessions are divided between the brothers, founding the Pasai line.
summary.zh: 珀拉克陷落，難民逃至三摩陀；蘇丹決為二子另建邦邑。乘象帕爾瑪提萬渡河，獵犬西帕塞吠叫示地——得一高丘，平整如人工鋪就；闢之建城，以犬之名『巴賽』名之。長子封為其王，王室象馬兵眾分而二之——巴賽王朝由此開基。

sensitivity.note: City-naming by hunting-dog; classic Southeast Asian foundation device.

passages.text: At this time the country of Perlac was conquered by its enemies, and the inhabitants took refuge in Samadra. Then Sultan Malec al Salih determined to found another settlement for his sons. Having mounted his elephant Parmadewan he crossed the river; his dog Sipasei gave tongue, and the Sultan quickly found an elevated ground of nearly the size of a palace and its appurtenances, very fine and smooth, as if it had been levelled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: He ordered this place to be cleared out and a negri or town founded there, a palace erected, and the whole to be named Pasei, after the prince's dog. He ordered his eldest son Malec al Zaher to be raja; and having divided his people, elephants, horses and royal accoutrements into two parts, he divided them between his sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
